snippet.title: Michael Jackson tried to destroy Thriller
snippet.description:
Did you know Michael almost destroyed Thriller?

On November 14, 1983, 43 years ago, Michael Jackson's Thriller was shown for the first time, at the Crest Theater in Los Angeles. Eddie Murphy shouted "Encore! Encore!" and they showed it twice.

Weeks before, leaders of the Jehovah's Witnesses, Michael's faith, told him the video promoted demonology and that he could be expelled. Michael called his lawyer, John Branca, and ordered the negatives destroyed. The production team locked them in Branca's office instead, and Branca suggested the note that still opens the video: "Due to my strong personal convictions, I wish to stress that this film in no way endorses a belief in the occult."

Sources: Michael Jackson, Making of Thriller footage, 1983 (clip used); Thriller official video (michaeljacksonVEVO, picture used); Wikipedia; Biography; Super Lawyers. The narrator's voice is synthetic.

Michael Jackson had invested heavily in Thriller and brought in director John Landis to create something far beyond the standard music video of the era. But the project created a collision between his work as an artist and his religious life as a Jehovah’s Witness. Under pressure from church elders, Michael eventually told his lawyer to destroy the film.

That’s where John Branca becomes the most interesting leadership example in the story. Instead of immediately carrying out a decision made during a crisis, Branca slowed things down. He protected the work, bought time, and searched for another option. Eventually, a disclaimer gave Michael a way to address his religious concerns without destroying the project.

There are two leadership lessons here that matter to founders and operators. First, surround yourself with excellent people. The people around a leader shouldn’t simply execute—they should have the judgment to recognize when a consequential decision deserves more thought.

Second, great decision-making sometimes means creating space before doing something irreversible. When emotions and stakes are high, the obvious choices can look binary: do this or do that. Strong executive leadership often means slowing the situation down long enough to discover a third option.

For me, that’s the practical management advice behind this story. Build a team with enough judgment to challenge the moment, give yourself time when a decision is difficult to reverse, and look for solutions that change the game instead of accepting the choices initially put in front of you.

snippet.title: Thriller Disclaimer
snippet.description:
A disclaimer at the beginning of Michael Jackson's "Thriller" music video states: 

"Due to my strong personal convictions, I wish to stress that this film in no way endorses a belief in the occult. - Michael Jackson.

"Why the Disclaimer Was Added

Religious Pressure: Jackson was a devout Jehovah's Witness at the time the video was filmed in 1983.

Threat of Excommunication: Church elders warned Jackson the video's horror imagery- specifically the werewolves and zombies- promoted demonology, which could get him expelled from the religion.

Near Destruction: Terrified of losing his faith, a distressed Jackson called his attorney, John Branca, and ordered him to destroy the film negatives.

Compromise: To protect the $900,000 investment and save the project, Branca suggested adding the text card to reassure church leaders and his mother that Jackson was not endorsing the occult.

The Closing Credit Gag

The video also features a lesser-known, humorous disclaimer at the very end of the credits:

 "All characters and events in this film are fictitious. Any similarity to actual events or persons living, dead, (or undead) is purely coincidental. 

The creation of "Thriller" was fueled by intense personal secrets, bizarre legal battles, and a complete clash between Michael Jackson's global fame and his deeply private, strict lifestyle.

Secrets & Scandals of "Thriller"

Secret Door-to-Door Preaching: 

Even at the height of Thriller's success, Jackson remained a dedicated Jehovah's Witness. 

He frequently wore disguises—including fake mustaches, wigs, and hats—to go door-to-door handing out religious literature in local neighborhoods without being recognized.

Funding  a "Fake" Documentary: 

The video's massive $900,000 budget was three times higher than any previous music video. 

Epic Records refused to pay for it, believing the song was just a "gimmick". 

To raise the money, Jackson and director John Landis sold the rights to a mock behind-the-scenes documentary called The Making of Michael Jackson's Thriller to MTV and Showtime, essentially getting the networks to finance the actual music video.

Real-Life Set Romance: Jackson cast Ola Ray, a former Playboy Playmate, as his co-star. 

Despite Jackson’s shy nature, the two shared a real-life, brief off-screen romance during the four-day shoot.

The "Tabasco Sauce" Eyes: To transform Jackson into a werewolf, makeup legend Rick Baker glued latex bladders to his face and inserted custom yellow scleral contact lenses. 

The lenses were so painful Jackson later noted it felt like having "Tabasco sauce in my eyes", but he endured the agonizing hours in the makeup chair to achieve the perfect look.

Secret Title: The track was not originally called "Thriller." Songwriter Rod Temperton initially wrote it as a cheerful pop track titled "Starlight". 

It was rewritten with horror themes at Jackson's request to fulfill his desire to create a theatrical, scary experience.

Surprising Clashes

A Childhood Fear: 

Despite playing a monster, Jackson hated horror movies in real life. 

His fear stemmed from a childhood trauma when his father, Joe Jackson, climbed through his bedroom window at night wearing a frightening mask and screaming, aiming to teach his children to lock their windows.

Final Breakdown with the Church: 

The compromise of the Thriller disclaimer only delayed the inevitable. 

In 1987, the church elders targeted Jackson again, criticizing his increasingly aggressive dancing, attendance at birthday parties, and his fascination with stage magic (which the church viewed as sorcery). 

Fed up with the restrictions on his creativity, Jackson officially disassociated himself from the Jehovah's Witnesses in 1987.

Post-Church Transformation: 

Former associates noted that cutting ties with his religion completely altered Jackson’s life trajectory. 

Without the strict moral boundaries of the faith keeping him anchored, Jackson isolated himself from much of his family, bought the Neverland Ranch, shifted toward radical changes in his physical appearance, and suffered from a growing dependence on prescription medication.

snippet.title: The most famous music video ever almost didn't exist — twice.
snippet.description:
The most famous music video ever almost didn't exist — twice.

▸ It started as "Starlight"
Songwriter Rod Temperton's first demo had a different title and chorus. He wrote Vincent Price's spoken-word section in a taxi on the way to the recording session.

▸ No budget
With two videos from the album already made, the label declined to pay for a third. Michael Jackson and director John Landis sold the rights to a "Making of Thriller" documentary to MTV and Showtime, raising about $500,000 — a record for a music video at the time (Rolling Stone, Billboard).

▸ "Destroy it"
Jackson, then a Jehovah's Witness, asked for the finished film to be destroyed after it caused trouble with his church. It was released with an on-screen disclaimer saying it did not endorse a belief in the occult. In 2009 it became the first music video selected for the U.S. National Film Registry (The Hollywood Reporter).

Why Making Thriller Nearly Broke Michael Jackson 

Michael Jackson nearly destroyed Thriller before the world ever heard it. Here is what actually happened inside the making of the greatest album ever recorded.

In 1982 Michael Jackson walked into Westlake Recording Studios with one goal — to make an album where every single song was a killer. What followed was nine months of creative warfare. Quincy Jones refused to put Billie Jean on the album. Engineer Bruce Swedien mixed the same song 91 times. CBS Records refused to fund the Thriller video. And two weeks before the most famous music video in history was due to premiere — Michael Jackson locked himself in his bedroom, refused to eat, and called his lawyer demanding the footage be destroyed.

This is the full story of the fights, the crises and the moments that almost stopped Thriller from existing — and what it cost Michael Jackson to bring it into the world.

snippet.description:
It was the autumn of 1982. The music world was on edge, but no one could have guessed that an eighteen-minute horror film on celluloid would change the industry forever. Michael Jackson had set his sights on Thriller, the title track of an album that was already breaking records. But Michael did not want an ordinary music video; he wanted a true cinematic movie in which he could transform into a bloodthirsty werewolf. The idea sounded brilliant, but panic struck at record label Epic Records, as this seemed like a financial and artistic nightmare. In the early eighties, music videos were nothing more than cheap promotional trailers costing around $50,000, used merely to boost record sales. Michael thought fundamentally differently after seeing the revolutionary short film An American Werewolf in London and demanded that the director of that film, John Landis, direct his music video. Landis was initially skeptical because he had never worked for a pop star, but Michael managed to convince him, after which the price tag quickly rose to a staggering $800,000, making it the most expensive music video in music history. The record company initially refused to contribute a single cent because the album had already been on the charts for months, but the determined Michael stood his ground and refused to work on future projects unless the budget was approved. What many do not know is that during negotiations, Michael was so obsessed with the script that he wrote scenes himself and designed the famous red jacket with designer Deborah Landis so that it would pop perfectly against the gray, dreary zombies. Ultimately, he convinced Showtime and MTV to split the costs, helped by the brilliant idea to produce a making-of documentary and sell it on videocassette, which generated a lucrative double revenue stream and unlocked the home video market forever. The shoot in Los Angeles was outright bizarre and full of risks because John Landis wanted the transformation to look terrifyingly realistic without computer graphics. Makeup wizard Rick Baker, who had previously won an Oscar for his work on the werewolf film, had to toil for days with liquid latex, pigskin, and mechanical prosthetics to give Michael a terrifying face, while Michael had to sit still in the chair for hours while the prosthetics were melted onto his face with glue. During production, a near-catastrophic moment occurred because Michael Jackson was a devout Jehovah's Witness at the time, and when church elders got wind of the project in which Michael turned into a werewolf and rose as a dancing zombie, they arrived on set furious. The church threatened to excommunicate Michael for promoting occult practices, causing the terrified pop star to immediately want to shut down production and destroy all props, until director John Landis desperately intervened and struck a brilliant legal compromise. snippet.title: Michael Jackson Thriller 4k #michaeljackson
snippet.description:
Michael Jackson - Thriller, 1983. Director - John Landis, choreographer - Michael Peters. A fourteen-minute short film built around a single song. At the time of its release, it was the longest music video in history and the first to be inducted into the U.S. National Film Registry.

This video almost never saw the light of day. Michael was a Jehovah's Witness, and the church was so opposed to demonic imagery that he wanted to destroy the original master tapes. John Landis talked him out of it. As a compromise, Michael personally wrote a disclaimer that appears at the beginning of the film:

"Due to my strongly held personal beliefs, I would like to emphasize that this film in no way promotes belief in the occult."

The werewolf makeup was created by Rick Baker, who had recently won an Oscar for his work on "An American Werewolf in London." Applying Michael's makeup took approximately six hours each day of filming.

Vincent Price recorded his famous final narration in just two takes. He was offered a choice between royalties and a flat fee. He chose the fee – around $20,000. The video subsequently earned hundreds of millions of dollars, and Price later called it one of the worst financial decisions of his life.

The film cost approximately half a million dollars to produce – a record for a music video at the time. To recoup the costs, Michael released the documentary The Making of Thriller on VHS, which became the best-selling home video in the world.

We've restored the most iconic footage in true 4K so you can see every line on the red jacket, every crease of the latex makeup, and every yellow eye. Michael transformed a horror film into a song the whole world wanted to dance to.

snippet.title: Why Michael Jackson Was Obsessed With Horror and Monsters
snippet.description:
🧟 Here's the part nobody expects: Michael Jackson was terrified of horror movies. In a 1999 MTV interview, he admitted it directly: "Believe it or not, I'm afraid to watch scary movies." And yet — the man who couldn't sit through a horror film spent three decades producing some of the most elaborate monster transformations, zombie choreography, and supernatural short films the music industry has ever seen.
In this video, we unpack exactly why Michael kept returning to horror despite being afraid of it — and what the monsters actually represented in his art:
The call that started everything:
▪️ Michael called John Landis in 1983 and said: "I want to turn into a monster. Can I do that?"
▪️ Landis later said: "He hadn't seen many horror films — he was scared of that stuff"
▪️ Michael didn't want to watch monsters. He wanted to become one.
Thriller (1983) — $500,000 budget:
▪️ Directed by John Landis (An American Werewolf in London)
▪️ Makeup effects by Rick Baker — first-ever Academy Award winner for Best Makeup
▪️ Vincent Price provided the iconic spoken-word narration
▪️ The Jehovah's Witness disclaimer: "This film in no way endorses a belief in the occult"
▪️ Nightmare Nostalgia called Thriller a "gateway to horror" that drove an entire generation to rent zombie and werewolf films
Captain EO (1986) — $17–23 million budget:
▪️ Produced by George Lucas, directed by Francis Ford Coppola
▪️ Anjelica Huston as the monstrous alien queen
▪️ Michael defeats the monsters not through violence — but through music and dance, transforming the ugly into the beautiful
▪️ Ran continuously at Disney parks worldwide from 1986 through 1997, revived in 2010
Ghosts (1996) — $15 million budget, paid personally by Michael:
▪️ Story co-written with Stephen King
▪️ Screenplay co-written by Mick Garris (Sleepwalkers, The Stand)
▪️ Directed by Stan Winston (Terminator 2, Jurassic Park, Aliens, Predator)
▪️ Cinematography by Russell Carpenter (Titanic)
▪️ 39-minute runtime — held the Guinness World Record for longest music video until 2013
▪️ Michael played five roles including the Mayor in full prosthetic white-face makeup
▪️ Screened at the 1997 Cannes Film Festival
▪️ The AV Club described it as an allegory for Michael's own life — a misunderstood "freak" driven out by a torch-wielding mob
Why transformation, not terror?
▪️ Every horror project Michael undertook centered on a person changing into something else
▪️ His own appearance changed dramatically through vitiligo, cosmetic procedures, and the 1984 Pepsi burns
▪️ The horror genre gave him a space where transformation was celebrated rather than pathologized
▪️ He specifically sought out the best monster-makers in the world — Rick Baker (7 Oscars), Stan Winston (4 Oscars) — and gave them budgets no music video had ever provided
The boy from Gary, Indiana who was afraid to watch scary movies ended up doing more for the visual language of horror than most actual horror directors ever accomplish. He just did it while moonwalking.
#MichaelJackson #Thriller #KingOfPop #MJ #MichaelJacksonGhosts #CaptainEO #StephenKing #StanWinston #RickBaker #HorrorHistory

Can I do that?", Landis telling Marc Lee "He hadn't seen many horror films — he was scared of that stuff," and Michael's 1999 MTV interview with Alex Colletti: "I'm afraid to watch scary movies"
Bloody Disgusting, "'Michael Jackson's Ghosts': The King of Pop's Overlooked Collaboration With Stephen King" (April 2026) — source for Stephen King story credit, Mick Garris co-writing, Stan Winston directing, Rick Baker's Thriller makeup, Vincent Price narration, and Ghosts screening at Cannes 1997

Sixty-six to seventy million copies.
No album in the history of recorded music has sold more. Not before Thriller. Not after it. Not in any genre, in any decade, by any artist.
He was twenty-four years old when he made it.

In Episode 3 of our Michael Jackson series, we go inside the making of the best-selling album in human history. The "Billie Jean" bassline that Quincy Jones initially wanted to cut. The Eddie Van Halen guitar solo recorded in a single take as a favor. The MTV color barrier broken by a threat from CBS Records. And the night of May 16, 1983 — the Motown 25 special, 47 million viewers, and the moonwalk that separated before from after in American popular culture.

We go inside the Thriller video — the fourteen-minute horror film that redefined what a music video could be, the Jehovah's Witness faith that produced the disclaimer at the beginning, the elaborate zombie choreography that John Landis and Michael built together.

And then we go inside January 27, 1984. The Pepsi commercial shoot. The pyrotechnics. The fire. The scalp burns. The prescription for pain medication.
The beginning of the end, started at the peak of the greatest beginning popular music had ever seen.

snippet.description:
A relação entre Michael Jackson e as Testemunhas de Jeová é uma das histórias mais complexas — e menos compreendidas — da cultura pop.

Neste vídeo, você vai entender como a conversão de Katherine Jackson mudou completamente o destino da família Jackson, inserindo dentro de casa uma estrutura religiosa rígida que moldou decisões pessoais, profissionais e emocionais por décadas.

Exploramos como Michael, no auge da fama mundial, tentou conciliar dois mundos incompatíveis: o de maior entertainer do planeta e o de um fiel profundamente comprometido com sua fé. Desde sair disfarçado para pregar de porta em porta até mudar suas performances por orientação de anciãos, sua devoção era real — mas constantemente testada.

O ponto de ruptura veio com Thriller, especialmente com o icônico videoclipe dirigido por John Landis. Considerado hoje um marco cultural, o projeto quase foi destruído pelo próprio Michael após pressão religiosa, que classificava o conteúdo como ocultismo.

Mas essa história vai além da música.

Você também vai conhecer o impacto dessas regras dentro da própria família — incluindo a ruptura emocional entre irmãos como LaToya Jackson, o caso da amiga que foi completamente excluída após questionar um ancião, e o funcionamento prático do ostracismo dentro da organização Testemunhas de Jeová.

No fim, esta não é apenas uma história sobre celebridade.

É um estudo profundo sobre fé, controle, pertencimento e o custo humano de tentar viver entre dois sistemas que não se conciliam.

snippet.title: THRILLER: il video che ha quasi DISTRUTTO la carriera di MICHAEL JACKSON
snippet.description:
Michael Jackson non ha mai cercato solo il successo: ha inseguito l'immortalità per curare la ferita di un'infanzia negata e il bruciante peso del pregiudizio. La sua storia è quella di un'ambizione titanica che nasce da un'umiliazione: la notte dei Grammy del 1980 quando, nonostante il trionfo di Off the Wall, si sentì ancora confinato nel recinto dorato della "musica black". Da quel pianto solitario scaturì una promessa gelida: creare un'opera così vasta da costringere il mondo intero a inginocchiarsi.

Nasce così Thriller, non un semplice album, ma un'arma di distruzione di massa culturale. Ispirandosi alla perfezione formale di Tchaikovsky e rifiutando la logica dei "filler" discografici, Michael trasforma le sue paranoie e il suo sangue in nove tracce leggendarie. Ma la vera rivoluzione avviene nell'ombra di una sala cinematografica, dove l'incontro con l'horror di John Landis accende l'intuizione definitiva: trasformare il videoclip da semplice promozione a evento sismico globale.

Il cortometraggio di Thriller è il racconto di una metamorfosi fisica e spirituale. Michael sfida la sua stessa fede come Testimone di Geova, rischiando la disassociazione e l'isolamento pur di dar voce alla "bestia" interiore, protetto solo da un cartello di smentita che era, in realtà, un grido d'aiuto. Tra sessioni di trucco estenuanti, lenti a contatto dolorose e un bluff finanziario che diede vita al primo "dietro le quinte" della storia, Jackson abbatte definitivamente l'apartheid televisiva di MTV, unificando il mondo sotto il ritmo di una danza macabra.

L'eredità di quel momento non sono solo gli otto Grammy del 1984 o le vendite da capogiro, ma la nascita del Re del Pop come icona universale. Michael Jackson ha dimostrato che il dolore può essere trasmutato in arte totale, ma quel successo ebbe un prezzo altissimo: una corona d'oro così pesante da schiacciare, col tempo, l'uomo fragile che cercava solo di essere amato da tutti.

snippet.title: M.Jackson Tried to Destroy the Thriller Video. His Religion Said It Was Evil.
snippet.description:
Michael Jackson tried to destroy the Thriller video. Two weeks before its premiere, he called his attorney and gave one order: burn the negatives. Everything. Gone.

This is the story they never told you.

Most people don't know that Michael Jackson didn't write a single word of Thriller. The man who wrote it was a British fish factory worker from a small English town — a man so private the music industry called him The Invisible Man. He came up with the title in a dream, and wrote Vincent Price's entire rap in a taxi on the way to the studio.

Vincent Price, for his part, recorded it in two or three takes — then chose a flat $20,000 fee over album royalties. Thriller sold 70 million copies.

And Michael Jackson almost destroyed all of it.

snippet.title: 50万ドルの賭け｜マイケルが『Thriller』MVを完成後『全部消して』と泣いた理由...マイケル・ジャクソン『涙の決断』
snippet.description:
【永遠の80's】マイケル・ジャクソン『Thriller』MVが音楽を映画にした夜
1983年12月2日、MTVで初放送された『Thriller』ミュージックビデオ。約14分という前代未聞の長さ、50万ドルという映画並みの制作費...しかし、このビデオは完成直後、一度は「全て破棄される予定」でした。
敬虔なエホバの証人の信仰を守りたいマイケルが、弁護士に「全てのネガフィルムを燃やしてくれ」と涙ながら命じた夜。ジョン・ランディス監督とマイケルの「命がけの決断」は、なぜ実現したのか。
■このビデオの見どころ
✅ 真夜中の電話から始まった伝説
映画『アメリカン・ウェアウルフ・イン・ロンドン』に魅了されたマイケルが、監督ジョン・ランディスに放った一言とは？
✅ 不可能な予算が生まれた秘密
CBSレコードに一度は拒否された50万ドル。未完成のビデオの「メイキング」を先に売却するという前代未聞の資金調達作戦。
✅ 涙の決断、そして奇跡の回生
破棄されそうになったネガフィルムを救った男。マイケルが「本当に？」と言った理由。
✅ ビデオ放映後の経済効果
2週間で700万枚のアルバム追加売上。MTV初放送で視聴率は10倍。7,000万枚売上『Thriller』アルバムの販売爆発の真犯人。
✅ MTV黒人差別からの解放
1983年、MTVで黒人アーティストのビデオはほぼ放映されていませんでした。『Thriller』が打ち破ったその壁。
✅ クリエイティブ・チームの秘話
衣装デザイナー・デボラ・ナドールマン・ランディス、振付師・マイケル・ピータース、メイクアップ・リック・ベイカー。映画史に名を刻む創作者たちが、わずか4日間で完成させた奇跡。
✅ 2つの時代、2つの変身
1950年代の映画館デート、1980年代の墓地...二重構造で観客を恐怖に陥れるストーリーテリング。
■重要な統計データ
🎬 制作費：50万ドル（当時のビデオ制作史上最高額）
🎬 撮影期間：4日間
🎬 ビデオの長さ：約14分
🎬 MTV初放送視聴率：10倍
🎬 2週間でのアルバム追加売上：700万枚
🎬 アルバム『Thriller』総売上：推定7,000万枚
🎬 メイキングVHS売上：100万本以上
🎬 YouTube再生数（2024年）：10億回突破
■主要クリエイター
【監督】ジョン・ランディス（John Landis）
『アメリカン・ウェアウルフ・イン・ロンドン』『Trading Places』などで知られる映画監督
【メイクアップ】リック・ベイカー（Rick Baker）
『アメリカン・ウェアウルフ・イン・ロンドン』で7時間の変身シーンを創作。映画史上最高峰のメイクアップアーティスト
【振付】マイケル・ピータース（Michael Peters）
『Thriller』の象徴的なゾンビダンスを創作。ビデオ内でも主役の真後ろで踊るゾンビとして出演
【衣装】デボラ・ナドールマン・ランディス（Deborah Nadoolman Landis）
『レイダース・ロスト・アーク』でハリソン・フォードのジャケットをデザイン。赤いジャケットの衣装デザイナー
【ナレーション】ビンセント・プライス（Vincent Price）

snippet.title: Michael Jackson Thriller 4k#michaeljackson #shorts #mjedit49s
snippet.description:
Michael Jackson - Thriller, 1983. Director -John Landis, choreographer - Michael Peters. A fourteen-minute short film built around a single song. At the time of its release, it was the longest music video in history and the first to be inducted into the U.S. National Film Registry.

This video almost never saw the light of day. Michael was a Jehovah's Witness, and the church was so opposed to demonic imagery that he wanted to destroy the original master tapes. John Landis talked him out of it. As a compromise Michael personally wrote adisclaimer that appears at the beginning of the film:

"Due to my strongly held personal beliefs, I would like to emphasize that this film in no way promotes belief in the occult."

The werewolf makeup was created by Rick Baker who had recently won an Oscar for hiswould like to emphasize that this film in no way promotes belief in the occult."

The werewolf makeup was created by Rick Baker, who had recently won an Oscar for his work on "An American Werewolf in London." Applying Michael's makeup took approximately six hours each day of filming.

Vincent Price recorded his famous final narration in just two takes. He was offered a choice between royalties and a flat fee. He chose the fee - around $20,000. The video subsequently earned hundreds of millions of dollars, and Price later called it one of the worst financial decisions of his life.

The film cost approximately half a million dollars to produce a record for a music video at the time. To recoup the costs, Michael released the documentary The Making of Thriller on VHS, which became the best-selling home video in the worldlater called it one of the  worst financial decisions of his life.



We've restored the most iconic footage in true 4K so you can see every line on the red jacket, every crease of the latex makeup, and every yellow eye. Michael transformed a horror film into a song the whole world wanted to dance to.
